content: Halitosis, commonly referred to as bad breath, is characterized by an unpleasant odor emanating from the mouth, often due to underlying oral or systemic conditions. It is a widespread issue, affecting approximately 50% to 60% of the global population, and can result in significant social stigma and diminished self-confidence. Various strategies have been employed to manage halitosis, including the use of mouthwashes, toothpastes, tongue scrapers, and even laser treatments. This Cochrane Review consolidates findings from previous reviews on tongue scraping and mouthrinses specifically for halitosis. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions targeting halitosis caused by oral diseases. Studies involving halitosis due to systemic conditions or interventions designed solely to mask bad breath were excluded. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults aged 16 years and older, comparing interventions for halitosis against placebo, no treatment, or other interventions. The interventions had to be administered for at least one week, with no upper limit on duration. Studies with quasi-randomized designs, follow-ups shorter than one week, or participants with advanced periodontitis were excluded. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, among others, up to April 2019. Ongoing trials were also identified through platforms like ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. A total of 44 trials involving 1809 participants were included in the review. The participants ranged in age from 17 to 77 years. Most studies reported short-term follow-up periods (one to four weeks), with only one study providing long-term follow-up data (three months). The risk of bias varied across studies, with three studies having a low risk of bias, 16 studies having a high risk, and 25 studies with unclear risk. The interventions were categorized into several types, including mechanical debridement, chewing gums, systemic deodorizing agents, topical agents, toothpastes, mouthrinses, tablets, and combination methods. The findings for each category are summarized below: 1. Mechanical Debridement: Evidence from two trials (46 participants) comparing tongue cleaning to no tongue cleaning was very uncertain. The dentist-reported organoleptic test (OLT) scores showed a mean difference (MD) of -0.20 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.34 to -0.07), but the certainty of evidence was very low. No data were available for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 2. Chewing Gums: One trial (65 participants) compared 0.6% eucalyptus chewing gum to placebo gum. The evidence was very uncertain, with a dentist-reported OLT score MD of -0.10 (95% CI: -0.31 to 0.11). No data were reported for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 3. Systemic Deodorizing Agents: One trial (40 participants) evaluated 1000 mg of champignon extract versus placebo. The evidence was very uncertain for patient-reported visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, with an MD of -1.07 (95% CI: -14.51 to 12.37). No data were available for dentist-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 4. Topical Agents: One trial (18 participants) assessed hinokitiol gel versus placebo gel. The evidence was very uncertain, with a dentist-reported OLT score MD of -0.27 (95% CI: -1.26 to 0.72). No data were reported for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 5. Toothpastes: One trial (81 participants) compared 0.3% triclosan toothpaste to a control toothpaste. The evidence was very uncertain, with a dentist-reported OLT score MD of -3.48 (95% CI: -3.77 to -3.19). No data were available for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 6. Mouthrinses: One trial (44 participants) evaluated a mouthwash containing chlorhexidine and zinc acetate versus a placebo mouthwash. The evidence was very uncertain, with a dentist-reported OLT score MD of -0.20 (95% CI: -0.58 to 0.18). No data were reported for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. 7. Tablets: No data were reported for key outcomes in this category. 8. Combination Methods: One trial (70 participants) compared brushing combined with cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash to brushing alone. The evidence was uncertain, with a dentist-reported OLT score MD of -0.48 (95% CI: -0.72 to -0.24). No data were available for patient-reported OLT scores or adverse events. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the effectiveness of interventions for managing halitosis was of low to very low certainty. This limited the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the superiority of any specific intervention or concentration. Future well-designed RCTs are needed, with standardized interventions and concentrations, to provide more robust evidence.
